draft.title: Revising for impact
card: Revising means rereading a draft as a reader would, then changing it to make it stronger. It is more than fixing spelling and punctuation.
Cut repetition
delete words, phrases or ideas that say the same thing twice. Keep a repeated word only when it is there on purpose, for effect.
Sharpen verbs
swap a weak or vague verb for a precise one. "She went across the yard" can become "She trudged across the yard", which also shows her mood.
Vary sentences
mix short and long sentences. A short sentence after a long one can slow the pace and stress a point. Then check that every part serves the piece's purpose, and cut or rework any part that does not.
draft.remember: Revise by asking of every word, sentence and paragraph: does this help the piece do its job?

a.q: Which change to a draft is an example of sharpening a verb?
opts: Changing "looked at" to "scrutinised" in a tense scene
Deleting a sentence that repeats the previous one
Adding a short sentence after two long ones
Fixing a spelling mistake in the final paragraph
a.why: Sharpening a verb means replacing a vague verb with a more precise one. The deleted sentence is cutting repetition, the short sentence is varying length, and the spelling fix is proofreading, not a change to the verbs.
a.clue: Look for the change that swaps one verb for a more exact one.

b.q: Mia is revising a descriptive piece about a storm. Every sentence is long, and a paragraph about her lunch has nothing to do with the storm. Which revision plan fits the card?
opts: Cut the lunch paragraph and add a few short sentences
Keep the lunch paragraph and make every sentence longer
Cut the lunch paragraph and join sentences into longer ones
Keep the lunch paragraph and fix the spelling instead
b.why: The lunch paragraph does not serve the purpose of the piece, so it should go, and short sentences would vary the rhythm and add punch. Joining sentences makes the sameness worse, because all the sentences are already long.
b.clue: Fix both problems: one part is off topic, and the sentence lengths are all the same.

a.best: Changing "looked at" to "scrutinised" in a tense scene

b.best: Cut the lunch paragraph and add a few short sentences

problems.detail: "A short sentence after a long one can slow the pace" clashes with common teaching. Short sentences are usually said to quicken the pace or create punch and impact, and the why for (b) itself says "add punch". Students may learn the effect backwards. Say instead that a short sentence after long ones can create a pause or emphasis.

The step of checking that every part serves the piece's purpose is tucked into the end of the "Vary sentences" bullet. This makes it look like part of sentence variety rather than a separate revision step, though question (b) relies on it.
